summary:
Raconteur examines the gap between organisational AI ambition and the workforce support needed to make it work, drawing on a Henley Business School AI pulse check survey and commentary from Professor Keiichi Nakata, Director of AI and Automation at Henley's World of Work Institute.

Key tension: worker confidence is rising (58% feel able to keep pace) yet 61% feel overwhelmed by the speed of change. Only 57% say their employer provides enough support to use AI effectively, and 60% say their organisation lacks AI use guidelines or are unsure whether any exist. Nakata argues employees are outpacing their employers, creating frustration.

Risks of this guidance vacuum: fragmented adoption where employees decide unilaterally how to use AI, inconsistent working practices, security and governance gaps, AI investments that fail to deliver value, and shadow AI as staff turn to accessible but unauthorised tools.

Persistent employee concerns are over-reliance on AI, skills erosion over time, and job security, though 58% remain optimistic about AI at work. Nakata says training must cover critical thinking and broader personal development, not just AI skills; equating AI readiness with technical proficiency alone risks creating new capability gaps.

Generational nuance: younger workers are more comfortable with AI-led management but more worried about job loss; older workers are less fearful for jobs but less comfortable being managed or directed by AI. Nakata cautions against over-indexing on age, since individual confidence varies. Support should be personalised by confidence, skills and role, with identified capability gaps and development pathways.

Work design: start with the work, then decide where AI fits, co-designing new ways of working rather than designing work around the technology, and clearly defining respective human and AI roles to reduce uncertainty.

Trust is decisive: 61% trust their organisation to consider their interests when introducing AI, but Nakata warns AI amplifies existing distrust, so leaders should build general trust first.
